blocks.text: Ammianus, book 22: He climbed Mount Casius, from which at the second cockcrow the first rising of the sun is seen. Others write that the sun is seen from Mount Casius at the fourth watch. Mela, book 1, ch. 10: So that from its highest summit it shows the rising of the sun from the fourth watch. Pliny, book 10, ch. 22: Casius, whose lofty height beholds the sun rising through the darkness at the fourth watch. Solinus: From whose summit the orb of the sun is seen while it is still the fourth watch. Martianus Capella, book 6: Casius, whose height sees the sun through the darkness at the fourth watch. Thus that second cockcrow and the fourth watch are the same. For cocks, on the authority of Pliny, go to bed with the sun, and at the fourth military watch call men back to their cares and labour. But although cocks crow twice in the depth of night, nevertheless, when something is read to have been done at the time of cockcrow without the addition of a number, the later one is always understood. It is so called κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν [kat᾽ exochēn], either because the cocks then crow more keenly and briskly; or because that later crowing is more useful to men, since it rouses them to the labours of the day; or finally because the time of the first cockcrow is designated by another name: for it is called μεσονύκτιον [mesonyktion], midnight, mid-night. [col. 121] Therefore not only Mark the Evangelist, but also Censorinus and Macrobius place cockcrow midway between midnight and morning, as has already appeared above. And Isidore (Orig. book 5, ch. 31) writes that cockcrow is so called on account of the cocks, the heralds of the light. Hence it is clear that only the later one is meant by him. In the words of Heliodorus too, book 1 of the Aethiopica, καθ᾽ ὃν καιρὸν ἀλεκτρυόνες ᾄδουσιν [kath᾽ hon kairon alektryones adousin], at the time [II, 690] when the cocks crow, the words that immediately follow show that the same thing is meant: that they crow αἰσθήσει φυσικῇ τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς περιστροφῆς ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόσρησιν κινουμένους [aisthēsei physikē tēs tou hēliou kath᾽ hēmas peristrophēs epi tēn tou Theou prosrēsin kinoumenous], stirred by a natural sense of the sun's turning towards us to salute God. And in Pollux too, among the last parts of the night is reckoned the time περὶ ἀλεκτρυόνων ᾠδὰς [peri alektryonōn ōdas] and ἀλεκτρυόνων ᾀδόντων [alektryonōn adontōn]. And Horace, Satire 1:
The man skilled in law and statutes praises the farmer's lot, when towards cockcrow a client knocks at his door.
